entities.name: Shwedagon Pagoda
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Shwedagon Pagoda is the most sacred Buddhist site in Myanmar and one of the most important Buddhist monuments in the world, located on Singuttara Hill in Yangon. Legend holds it was founded over 2,500 years ago, though the oldest verifiable records date from the 14th century. The main stupa rises 98 meters and is covered in 27 metric tons of gold plates with a diamond bud containing 4,531 diamonds, making it one of the world's most valuable religious structures.

Myanmar's kings competed to add gold and precious gems to the pagoda, establishing a tradition of royal donation that transformed it into a treasury of Buddhist religious art. King Bayinnaung (16th century) donated his own weight in gold; King Hsinbyushin raised the stupa to its current height in 1774. The platform surrounding the main stupa contains 64 smaller stupas and dozens of pavilions donated by donors across centuries.

Shwedagon Pagoda became a focal point of Burmese nationalism: British colonial occupation of the pagoda compound (1824-1826 and 1852-1929) was deeply resented. Mahatma Gandhi urged the British to leave the pagoda. The 1988 protests against Myanmar's military regime began near the pagoda, as did Aung San Suu Kyi's first major speech to 500,000 people in 1988. The 2007 Saffron Revolution of Buddhist monks used the pagoda as gathering point, connecting religious and political resistance.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Shwedagon Pagoda's spiritual and political centrality to Myanmar — as the holiest Buddhist site and the focal point of anti-colonial and pro-democracy movements — makes it the defining monument of Burmese civilization.
